column3: The Hebrew describes becoming Pharaoh’s son-in-law and taking his daughter in separate clauses, without an explicit introductory “Later.” It calls Solomon’s residence a house, where BSB uses “palace.”
The Hebrew explicitly says “until those days.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew asks what God should give; BSB makes this a promise, “I will give it to you.”
The Hebrew coordinates preserving the great kindness and giving a son with “and”; BSB makes the gift the means with “by giving.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew refers to the chosen people as “Your people”; BSB leaves the possessive implicit.
The Hebrew names a listening heart and repeats judging in the final question; BSB uses “understanding heart” and then “govern.”
The Hebrew locates the pleasing matter in the Lord’s eyes.
The Hebrew speaks of many days and the enemies’ soul, where BSB uses long life and death. It describes understanding to hear judgment; BSB has discernment to administer justice.
The Hebrew describes doing and giving with completed verb forms; BSB uses “I will do” and “I will give.”
The Hebrew speaks of having given and compares him with a man among kings; BSB uses “I will give” and “no man in any kingdom.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says he came to Jerusalem; BSB makes this a return.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats the house at the end.
The Hebrew calls any additional person a stranger and repeats “in the house.”
The Hebrew says she lay on him; BSB specifies rolling over on him.
The Hebrew calls the sleeping woman “your maidservant”; BSB uses “I.”
The Hebrew repeats “in the morning” and twice presents the findings with “behold”; BSB uses discovering and realizing.
The Hebrew calls the second speaker “this one” and says they spoke; BSB calls her the first woman and specifies that they argued.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says they brought the sword before the king; BSB says they brought him a sword.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew intensifies the prohibition of killing by repeating the verb root; BSB says “Do not kill him!”
The Hebrew says “give her” without explicitly identifying “the first woman”; BSB supplies that identification. It introduces the verdict with answering and saying.
Close to the Hebrew.
